newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Japan's plans to cut dependence on oil optimistic.
newsitem.headline: Japan's plans to cut dependence on oil optimistic.

text.p: Japanese oil executives said on Monday Tokyo's plans to cut dependence on fossil fuels for environmental reasons were too optimistic and doubted the targets would be met.

Plans to increase dependence on nuclear energy in the next century "will be delayed" and the set targets "are too optimistic", said Kazuhisa Hayashi, manager of Showa Shell Sekiyu KK Change Promotion Center.
Hayashi, addressing a seminar in Kuwait, said a June 1994 outlook by the government envisaged a rise in nuclear power production to 70.5 million kilo watt (MKW) in 2010 from 41.1 MKW in 1995.

"The forecast for the supply of nuclear power and new types of energy is over-optimistic," he added. Reminding delegates of the first atomic bomb on Hiroshima in 1945, Hayashi said the Japanese people were "very sensitive" about nuclear power.

Tsunekazu Nakajima, General Manager of the Planning Department at Kashima Oil Co Ltd, said many doubted the government's forecast would be realised. He said Japan was revising its long term primary energy supply outlook, expecting it to forecast a drop in oil's share to 47 percent in 2010 from 57.
But "Those of us in the oil industry believe that Japan will still depend on oil for more than half of its primary energy supply even in the year 2010," he added.

Japanese industry executives said Tokyo imports 80 percent of its primary energy supply -- the highest level by any of the major developed countries. It imports almost all of its 4.5 million barrels per (bpd) crude needs, with 80 percent coming from Middle Eastern states.

The United Arab Emirates is Japan's largest supplier, accounting for 27 percent of its crude imports followed by Saudi Arabia's 22.5 percent, including 100,000 bpd from the Neutral Zone which the kingdom shares with Kuwait.

Including another 100,000 bpd of crude from the zone, Kuwait supplies Tokyo with 7.5 percent of its needs. Kuwaiti officials said the Gulf Arab state also exports to Japan 980,000 tonnes of LPG and 2.7 million tonnes of Naphtha.
Non-Arab Iran accounts for 10 percent while Qatar and Oman each contribute six percent to Japan's crude needs.

Nakajima said: "In order to...achieve the policy targets in the government's plan to prevent global warming, the new forecast will require that various types of energy conservation are promoted, that new types of wind, solar and other alternative energy sources are developed and that many nuclear power plants are built."

The seminar was organised by the state Kuwait Petroleum Corporation (KPC) and the Petroleum Energy Center, a Japanese incorporated foundation set up in 1986 to research and develop new technologies for the petroleum industry.
